hero.prompt: A friendly flat cartoon of an empty wooden school bench holding one blue light microscope and two clean glass slides, plain soft background.
hero.alt: A school science bench with a light microscope and two glass slides

slides.title: Are bacteria built like Amina's skin cells?
slides.subtitle: Write alone and in silence first.
slides.time_note: Silent writing 2 minutes. Callback and prompt take the first 20 seconds.

blocks.text: A girl smiling and holding up one finger with a neat plaster on it, beside a chopping board with sliced onions.
items: amina_healing_finger

A friendly flat cartoon of one teenage girl in a school uniform smiling and holding up one hand with a neat plaster on her finger, standing beside a kitchen table with a wooden chopping board of sliced onions.

blocks.text: Is E. coli built like Amina's skin cells, or differently? Give two reasons.

do: Say the callback to Lesson 2.
Write the focus question and the writing prompt on the board.
Students open their science notebooks and write alone. No talking.
Start the 2-minute timer.
Walk the room silently. Scan 8–10 notebooks while students write.
Do not correct any idea.
say: Last lesson we said a cell is the basic unit of life. But are all cells built the same way? Let us think about this carefully.
When Amina cut her finger slicing onions in Nairobi, bacteria from the onion skin or the blade could enter the wound.

Amina is worried about bacteria entering her cut. Do you think a bacterium like E. coli is built the same way as Amina's skin cells, or differently? Open your notebook. Write alone and in silence. Give two reasons for your prediction. You have two minutes.
notes.wait_time: Stay silent for the full 2 minutes of writing.
look_for: In 8–10 notebooks: does the student use Lesson 2 words (nucleus, membrane, organelles) or only everyday words like small?
Does every student give two reasons, not only yes or no?
Note how much scaffolding the Observe phase will need.
if_then: If a student stares at the page, say: Think about size and what is inside a cell. Write what you remember from Lesson 2.
If a student asks whether it is right, say: There is no right or wrong yet. Write your best idea and your reasons.
notes.why_this_works: Writing a prediction with reasons before any teaching shows what students already think. It gives them an idea they want to test. Common misconception: all living cells are built the same way. This slide lets that idea appear now.
answer_key: Sample prediction: I think E. coli is built differently from Amina's skin cells. Reason 1: bacteria are much smaller. Reason 2: I think a bacterium has no nucleus, so it is simpler. Any prediction with two reasons is accepted. Do not correct it yet.

slides.title: Share with your shoulder partner
slides.subtitle: Tell your partner what you wrote and why.

items: people :: Turn to your shoulder partner
speech :: Read your prediction and your two reasons
ear :: Listen to your partner's reasons

do: Start the 1-minute timer.
Listen to 4–5 pairs as you walk.
Choose three students from the class register for the next slide. Choose one who predicted the same, one who predicted differently, and one you have not heard from today.
say: Turn to your shoulder partner. Share what you wrote. You have one minute.
notes.wait_time: Let pairs talk for the full minute. Stop them at 1 minute.
notes.why_this_works: Saying an idea aloud to one partner is low risk. More students are then ready to share with the whole class.

slides.title: BEFORE — Our Predictions
slides.subtitle: Three classmates share. All ideas stay open.
slides.time_note: Three students share; the teacher scribes key words.

blocks.text: Are the bacteria that could infect Amina's cut built the same way as her body cells?
We will test every prediction today.
items: No ideas are right or wrong yet.

do: Draw a box on the board titled BEFORE — Our Predictions.
Cold-call the three students you chose from the register.
Write their key words in the box. Do not comment on them.
Say the closing line.
say: Thank you. I will write your key words here. We will not say right or wrong yet.
By the end of this lesson we will have enough evidence to confirm or revise every one of these predictions. Let us go and find out.
notes.wait_time: 5 seconds after each cold-call before you prompt.
look_for: Key words you hear. Students usually say smaller, simpler or no nucleus.
Do predictions use Lesson 2 vocabulary or only everyday words?
Write down which ideas the Observe phase will test.
if_then: If a student gives only an opinion, say: What is your reason? Tell us one thing you remember from Lesson 2.
If a student asks whether they were right, say: Keep that question. We will find out with evidence today.
If no student predicts a nucleus difference, do not add it. Write only what students say.
notes.why_this_works: Writing predictions on the board makes thinking visible and creates a record to return to. Not correcting keeps students curious and ready to test their ideas.

slides.title: E. coli: how is it built?
slides.subtitle: A bacterium linked to food poisoning from nyama choma left out too long.

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.
Wall: peptidoglycan. DNA: circular, nucleoid region. Size: 1–5 micrometres.

do: Project this slide. If you can, also give each group a printed copy of this diagram and the next one.
Explain where E. coli is linked to food poisoning.
Point to each label slowly. Do not explain what the features mean yet.
say: E. coli is a bacterium. In Kenya, it has been linked to food poisoning cases from nyama choma that is left out too long at a roadside kiosk in Nairobi or Mombasa.
It is very small, about 2 micrometres. Amina would not see it, but her white blood cells would find it.
Now let us look carefully at how it is built compared to her own cheek cell.
if_then: If the class has no printed copies, say: Look at the screen. We will come back to these two diagrams when you fill in your table.
notes.why_this_works: Starting from a real Kenyan food-safety context makes bacteria feel real and important before students analyse the drawing.

slides.title: Human cheek cell: how is it built?
slides.subtitle: A cell from the inside of your cheek.
slides.time_note: Show the second diagram in 1 minute.

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.
Also: nuclear membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes, rough ER. Size: 10–100 micrometres.

do: Put the two diagrams side by side if you can: printed copies, or flip between this slide and the E. coli slide.
Point to the labels. Do not explain them.
say: This is a human cheek cell. It is the cell you would scrape from the inside of your cheek.
Look at the labels. In a minute you will compare it with E. coli.
if_then: If students ask what a nuclear membrane is, say: Look at your diagram. What do you see around the nucleus?
notes.why_this_works: Showing both cells in the same style lets students compare features directly from the drawings, with no teacher telling.

slides.title: Watch me read one row
slides.subtitle: I show you how. Then it is your turn.
slides.time_note: Think-aloud for the first feature only.

items: magnifier :: Pick one feature: membrane-bound nucleus.
eyes :: Look at E. coli. Find the DNA.
question :: Is there a membrane around it?
pencil :: Write only what the diagram shows.

do: Go back to the E. coli diagram if needed and point to the DNA as you think aloud.
Model the first feature only.
Tell students to draw the table in their notebooks if there is no printed copy.
say: I look at the E. coli diagram. I can see DNA here. But is there a membrane around it? No. So I write: no membrane-bound nucleus.
Now you complete the rest. Use the diagrams only. Work alone.
if_then: If students ask for help, say: Use the same steps. Find the feature, look at the diagram, write what you see.
notes.why_this_works: A short think-aloud shows students how to read a diagram without giving away all the answers.

slides.title: Your turn: complete the table
slides.subtitle: Work alone. Use the diagrams only.
slides.time_note: Individual work 4 minutes. No teacher input.

do: Students need the table in their notebooks, pre-printed or drawn. Copies of both diagrams should be on each desk, or flip back to the two diagram slides.
Start the 4-minute timer.
Walk silently. Look at tables. Do not correct.
Note two or three misconceptions to use in the review.
say: Work alone. Use the diagrams only. I will not help during this time. You have four minutes.
notes.wait_time: Stay silent for the full 4 minutes.
look_for: Check 8–10 tables.
Do students tell the nucleoid region apart from a membrane-bound nucleus?
Do students see that ribosomes are in both cells?
Does the size row have units (micrometres)?
if_then: If a student writes that E. coli has no DNA, say: Look at the E. coli diagram again. What is labelled near the middle?
If a student says E. coli has no ribosomes, say: Find ribosomes on both diagrams. Are they the same in both?
If a student leaves a cell empty, say: Write what you can see on the diagram. Put a question mark if you are not sure.
notes.why_this_works: A table asks every student to look at the same features. Working alone first means each student thinks before the partner and class talk. Misconception: ribosomes are membrane-bound organelles.
answer_key: Membrane-bound nucleus: E. coli — no; cheek cell — yes.
Membrane-bound organelles: E. coli — no (it has ribosomes, which are not membrane-bound); cheek cell — yes (for example mitochondria and rough endoplasmic reticulum).
Size: E. coli — about 1–5 micrometres; cheek cell — about 10–100 micrometres.
Cell wall: E. coli — present, made of peptidoglycan; cheek cell — absent.
Genetic material: E. coli — circular DNA in the nucleoid region, free in the cytoplasm, no nuclear membrane; cheek cell — inside the nucleus, which has a nuclear membrane.
notes.science_note: Ribosomes are in both cell types. They are not surrounded by a membrane, so they are not membrane-bound organelles.

slides.title: Compare with your partner
slides.subtitle: Disagree on a row? Put a small question mark.

items: people :: Compare your table with your partner
check :: Same answer? Good
question :: Different answer? Put a small ? beside that row

do: Start the 1-minute timer.
Listen to pairs. Note which rows get question marks.
say: Compare your table with your partner. If you disagree on any row, put a small question mark. We will sort it out together.
notes.wait_time: Let pairs talk for the full minute.
look_for: Which rows have most question marks? Plan to ask about those first in the review.
if_then: If a pair does not disagree on anything, say: Explain to each other where on the diagram you found each answer.
notes.why_this_works: Partner talk lets students test their answers in a safe space before the whole-class review.

slides.title: Class review: row by row
slides.subtitle: Say which part of the diagram shows your answer.
slides.time_note: Quick cold-call review of five rows.

blocks.text: What did you write, and where on the diagram can you see it?

items: target :: Membrane-bound nucleus?
factory :: Membrane-bound organelles?
ruler :: Approximate size
house :: Cell wall: present or absent?
dna :: Where is the genetic material?

do: Go through the five rows. Cold-call a different student for each row from the register.
Choose students whose partner talk showed a question mark on that row.
Confirm correct answers. Fix misconceptions straight away.
say: Wanjiku, what did you write for membrane-bound organelles in E. coli? Show us on the diagram.
Thank you. Who agrees? Who wrote something different?
notes.wait_time: At least 5 seconds before you prompt.
look_for: Can students point to the part of the diagram that gives the answer?
Does the class now agree that ribosomes are in both cells?
Do students separate nucleoid region from nucleus?
if_then: If a student says ribosomes are organelles E. coli does not have, say: Look at the E. coli diagram. Are ribosomes labelled? Ribosomes are in both cells. They are not membrane-bound.
If a student says the cheek cell has a cell wall, say: Look at the cheek cell diagram. Is a cell wall labelled?
If time runs out, keep the rows with most question marks.
notes.why_this_works: Calling students from the register means everyone must be ready. Asking where on the diagram they see the answer keeps the class using evidence, not guessing.
answer_key: Use the answer key for the table on the Your turn slide.

slides.title: Cold-call round: show your thumb
slides.subtitle: Listen to each answer. Then show what you think.

blocks.text: Do you agree, partly agree or disagree — and why?

items: check :: Thumb up: I agree
hand :: Thumb sideways: I partly agree
cross :: Thumb down: I disagree

do: Point to the BEFORE — Our Predictions box on the board so students can see what they predicted.
Call five students from the register, not volunteers. Use a different group, seating zone and gender for each if you can.
Ask each student a different question. Questions go from identification to explanation to application.
After each answer, ask the class for thumbs. Then ask one student with a sideways or down thumb why.
say: Ochieng, look at the E. coli diagram. What is the name of the region where its DNA is found, and why is it different from the nucleus in the cheek cell?
Fatuma, E. coli has ribosomes AND the cheek cell has ribosomes. Does that make them the same type of cell? Explain your thinking.
Kamau, give me one feature from your table that is DIFFERENT between the two cells and explain what that difference means.
Aisha, the cheek cell is about 50 times bigger than E. coli. Why might a larger cell need membrane-bound organelles when a smaller cell does not?
Brian, Amina is worried about bacteria in her cut. Based on what we have just learned, are those bacteria prokaryotes or eukaryotes? How do you know?
Thumbs: do you agree, partly agree, or disagree? Anyango, why did you put your thumb sideways?
notes.wait_time: 5 seconds for questions 1, 3 and 5; 7 seconds for question 2; 8 seconds for question 4.
look_for: Check the thumbs for all five answers. Is the whole class agreeing or split?
Can students explain, not only name? Listen for because.
Is the ribosome misconception resolved? Watch the thumbs after question 2.
Student 5 should link the bacteria in the cut to the structure in the table.
if_then: If Student 1 has no response after 5 seconds, say: Look at the label on the diagram. What does it say near the DNA?
If Student 2 says yes, they are the same, say: Ribosomes are in both. Now look at the rest of your table. Are the two cells the same in everything else?
If Student 4 gives a reasonable idea, accept it. Question 4 has no single right answer.
If thumbs are mostly down or sideways, say: Let us look at the diagram again. Who can point to the evidence?
notes.why_this_works: Escalating questions move students from recall to reasoning. Thumbs signalling makes every student judge their classmates' answers, not just the student called on.
answer_key: Student 1: The region is the nucleoid region. The DNA lies free there with no membrane around it. In the cheek cell the DNA is inside a nucleus that has a nuclear membrane.
Student 2: No. Both cells have ribosomes, but ribosomes are not membrane-bound. E. coli has no membrane-bound organelles. The cheek cell does.
Student 3: Example: E. coli has no membrane-bound nucleus but the cheek cell has one. So the cheek cell keeps its DNA in its own compartment.
Student 4: Accept reasonable reasoning, for example: a bigger cell has more jobs to do, and organelles with membranes keep different jobs separate.
Student 5: They are prokaryotes. E. coli has no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles, it has a cell wall and it is very small.

items: microbe :: Sentence 1: One feature that makes E. coli a prokaryote.
mouth :: Sentence 2: One feature that makes the cheek cell a eukaryote.
bandage :: Sentence 3: Why this difference matters for Amina's healing cut.

do: Start the 3-minute timer.
Walk the room. Read 4–5 notebooks over shoulders. Do not collect books.
Mark in your head which students wrote only definitions.
say: Now write three sentences in your notebook. I will give you three minutes.

Sentence 1: one structural feature that makes E. coli a prokaryote. Sentence 2: one structural feature that makes the cheek cell a eukaryote. Sentence 3: why this difference matters for the healing-cut story.
notes.wait_time: Stay silent for the full 3 minutes.
look_for: Check 4–5 notebooks.
Does Sentence 3 link to Amina's cut and not only repeat a definition?
Is the feature in each sentence correct (no membrane-bound nucleus; has a membrane-bound nucleus)?
if_then: If Sentence 3 is only a definition, say: What does this have to do with Amina's cut? Which cells are in the wound, and which cells could get in?
If a student writes only they are different, say: Different in what way? Use a word from your table.
If a student finishes early, say: Add one more difference from your table.
notes.why_this_works: Writing forces each student to put the idea into their own words. Linking Sentence 3 to the healing cut keeps the science tied to the anchor phenomenon. Misconception: bacteria and body cells are the same kind of cell.
answer_key: Sentence 1: E. coli is a prokaryote because its DNA is not inside a membrane-bound nucleus; it lies free in the nucleoid region.
Sentence 2: The cheek cell is a eukaryote because its DNA is inside a nucleus with a nuclear membrane, and it has membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria.

Sentence 3: This matters for Amina's cut because the bacteria that could infect it are prokaryotes with a different structure from her own eukaryotic body cells, so her white blood cells can find and deal with them.

slides.title: Words that carry their meaning
slides.subtitle: Copy both words and their Greek roots.
slides.time_note: Teacher writes the roots; students copy.

items: Prokaryote :: pro = before. karyon = nucleus. Meaning: before nucleus.
Eukaryote :: eu = true. karyon = nucleus. Meaning: true nucleus.

blocks.text: Let the Greek roots remind you what the words mean.

do: Write both words and their roots on the board.
Students copy them as a memory anchor.
Say the words aloud. Ask the class to repeat them.
say: These words carry their meaning inside them. Prokaryote: before nucleus. Eukaryote: true nucleus.
Every time you see these words, let the Greek roots remind you what they mean.
look_for: Check 3–4 notebooks for correct copying of pro, eu and karyon.
if_then: If a student asks why a prokaryote has no nucleus in the name, say: Look at your table. Where is the DNA in E. coli?
notes.why_this_works: Naming the words after students have seen the evidence gives the words a meaning to attach to. Greek roots help students remember them.
answer_key: Prokaryote: pro = before, karyon = nucleus, so before nucleus.
Eukaryote: eu = true, karyon = nucleus, so true nucleus.

slides.title: Driving Question Board: what did we wonder?
slides.subtitle: Look at our Lesson 1 questions.
slides.time_note: Teacher reads wonder notes; 20 seconds partner talk.

blocks.text: A classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes with small gold stars beside some of them.
items: dqb_sticky_notes_board
A friendly flat cartoon of a classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes, with three small gold stars stuck beside some notes, and a wooden desk with a pot of pencils in front.

blocks.text: Can we now answer one Lesson 1 wonder question?

do: Stand at the Driving Question Board.
Read aloud two or three Lesson 1 wonder notes that today's work can now partly or fully answer. For example: Why are some cells bigger than others? Are germs the same as cells?
Give 20 seconds of partner talk.
Take a quick thumbs vote: does the evidence from today's diagrams and table support an answer?
say: In Lesson 1, some of you wondered whether bacteria and human cells are the same thing. Let us look. (Read the wonder note aloud.)
Can we now answer that? Turn to your partner. You have 20 seconds.
Thumbs up if today's evidence supports an answer. Thumbs sideways if it partly does. Thumbs down if it does not.
look_for: Do students use evidence from the table or diagrams (for example nucleus or size), or only opinion?
Count thumbs. Is the class mostly up, sideways or down?
if_then: If students say yes with no reason, say: What did you see in the diagrams that tells you?
If no wonder note fits, choose a note about size or about germs and cells and read that. Do not invent a new student question.
notes.why_this_works: Going back to the students' own Lesson 1 questions shows them how much they have learned. A vote makes them judge whether evidence supports a claim.

slides.title: Write what we know and still wonder
slides.subtitle: Write two sentences. Then post them on the board.

blocks.text: A: We now know that prokaryotes and eukaryotes differ in…
items: B: But we still wonder…
Say HOW they differ.

do: Give each student a sticky note, or a small piece of paper.
Write Sentence A and Sentence B on the board.
Start the 2-minute timer.
Students post their notes on the Driving Question Board in two columns: WHAT WE NOW KNOW and WHAT WE STILL WONDER.
While students post, scan the KNOW column. Read 6–8 notes.
say: You have two minutes to write both sentences and post them on the board.
Do not just write they are different. Write HOW they are different, using words from your table.
notes.wait_time: Full 2 minutes for writing and posting.
look_for: Scan 6–8 KNOW notes. Do they use structure words (nucleus, organelles, cell wall) or only general words like bigger or more complex?
Does the KNOW note rest on something students saw today (the diagrams or table)?
Are WONDER notes real questions, not statements?
if_then: If a note says they are different, say: Different how? Look at your table and write one difference.
If a student cannot think of a wonder, say: What would you like to know about the parts inside the cheek cell?
If most KNOW notes use only everyday words, plan to revisit the table words at the start of Lesson 4.
notes.why_this_works: Separating what we know from what we wonder trains students to tell evidence-based claims from open questions. The words in the KNOW notes show whether the table work worked.
answer_key: A: We now know that prokaryotes and eukaryotes differ in whether they have a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, and in size.
B: But we still wonder what the organelles inside a eukaryotic cell do.

slides.title: Gallery scan: our wonder questions
slides.subtitle: Three classmates read one WONDER note each.

items: WHAT WE NOW KNOW :: Notes that start: We now know that…
WHAT WE STILL WONDER :: Notes that start: But we still wonder…

blocks.text: Hold onto these questions. We will investigate them next.

do: Students look at the board for a short gallery scan.
Choose three WONDER notes with different ideas.
Read each one aloud, or ask its writer to read it.
Mark them as flagged questions for Lessons 4 and 5.
say: These are excellent questions. They are exactly what we will investigate in Lessons 4 and 5, when we go inside the organelles of plant and animal cells.
Hold onto these questions.
look_for: Do the flagged questions ask about what organelles do?
Are students pleased or worried about not knowing yet?
if_then: If a student says they have no questions left, say: Look at the WONDER column. Which question would you like answered first?
notes.why_this_works: Reading wonder notes aloud shows that not yet knowing is valued. It keeps the class story moving forward.

slides.title: Model Building: add a new panel
slides.subtitle: Draw E. coli and a cheek cell side by side.
slides.time_note: Drawing and labelling 3 minutes. Give the task in under 30 seconds.

items: Open Version 1. Add a new panel.
Draw both cells side by side.
Label four or more features.
Red :: Prokaryote only
Blue :: Eukaryote only
Black :: Both

do: Write the colour code on the board.
Students open their Version 1 model from Lesson 2 and add the new panel beside or below it.
Start the 3-minute timer. The drawing and caption together take 5 minutes.
Walk the room. Ask probing questions of 6–8 students.
Check that ribosomes are drawn in black.
say: Your cumulative cell model is growing. In Lesson 2 you drew a generalised cell. Today you add a new panel showing both cell types side by side, with the differences clearly annotated.
This is not just copying. You are building a model that explains. Use the colour code: red for prokaryote only, blue for eukaryote only, black for both.
You have not labelled the nucleoid region on your E. coli. Is that because E. coli has no DNA, or because the DNA is arranged differently?
notes.wait_time: Stay quiet for most of the time. Ask a probing question to one student at a time.
look_for: Check 6–8 models.
Are ribosomes black (in both), not red or blue?
Does each model have four or more labels from the table?
Is the colour code used to compare, not only to label?
if_then: If ribosomes are red or blue, say: Check your table. Are ribosomes in both cells?
If a student draws a cell wall on the cheek cell, say: Look at your table. Does the cheek cell have a cell wall?
If a student leaves out the DNA of E. coli, say: Look at the E. coli diagram. Where is its DNA?
notes.why_this_works: A model that is revised each lesson makes growth in thinking visible. The colour code makes students judge what is different and what is shared, not just label. Misconception: ribosomes are membrane-bound organelles.
answer_key: Model: two outline drawings side by side. E. coli: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, circular DNA in the nucleoid region (red for cell wall and nucleoid; black for ribosomes, cell membrane, cytoplasm). Cheek cell: cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus with nuclear membrane, mitochondria, rough endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes (blue for nucleus, mitochondria, rough endoplasmic reticulum; black for ribosomes, cell membrane, cytoplasm).

slides.title: Caption and evidence
slides.subtitle: Finish your new panel with a caption.

blocks.text: A prokaryote has no membrane-bound nucleus, while a eukaryote does — and this difference matters because…
items: This model is based on evidence from…

do: Write the caption stem on the board.
Students write the caption and the evidence sentence under their two drawings.
Walk the room. Read 6–8 captions.
say: Finish your panel. Complete the caption. Then say where your evidence came from.
Do not just write they are different. Why does it matter?
notes.wait_time: Stay quiet while students write. Ask one probing question at a time.
look_for: Check 6–8 captions.
Does the caption give a correct consequence (for example, the DNA is kept in its own compartment), or is it blank or only they are different?
Does the evidence sentence name the diagrams or the table?
Flag students with blank captions for re-engagement in Lesson 4.
if_then: If the caption says only they are different types, say: Why does it matter? What does a nucleus do for the DNA?
If the evidence sentence is missing, say: What did you look at today? Write it after: This model is based on evidence from.
If a student has no idea, say: Think about where the DNA is in each cell. How might that change what the cell can do?
notes.why_this_works: Finishing the sentence with a reason moves students from recall to explaining. Citing evidence links the model to what they saw today. Misconception: the difference between cells is only cosmetic.
answer_key: Caption: A prokaryote has no membrane-bound nucleus, while a eukaryote does — and this difference matters because the nucleus keeps the DNA in its own compartment, which helps the cell do more complex jobs.
Evidence: This model is based on evidence from the E. coli and cheek cell diagrams and our comparison table.

slides.title: Share a model and look ahead
slides.subtitle: Two classmates show their models. Then write one prediction.
slides.time_note: Two quick shares, then one sentence.

blocks.text: Next lesson we go inside a plant cell. Remember Amina's onion: it is a plant.
items: Write one sentence: Next lesson I predict that a plant cell will have… because…

do: Choose two students whose models showed strong annotations. Ask each to hold up their model.
Ask each to say one annotation they are proud of and why.
Students write one prediction sentence for the next lesson.
say: Wanjiru, hold up your model and tell us one annotation you are proud of and why.

Next lesson we go inside the eukaryotic cell, and we start with the plant cell. Remember the onion that Amina was cutting when she hurt her finger. That is a plant. Its cells will be our starting point.
Write one sentence: Next lesson I predict that a plant cell will have… because…
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds for the prediction sentence before you collect ideas.
look_for: Do the two shared models show precise annotations?
Does the prediction sentence give a reason, not just a guess?
if_then: If a student cannot predict, say: Think about the cheek cell. What do you think a plant cell shares with it?
If time is short, ask students to finish the prediction sentence at home.
notes.why_this_works: A low-stakes share sets a standard of precision and celebrates good work. A prediction for the next lesson gives students a reason to come back curious.
answer_key: Sample prediction: Next lesson I predict that a plant cell will have a nucleus and other organelles because it is a eukaryote like the cheek cell.

build_log.sow_says: Unit data: "Sub-Strand 1.3: Cell Structure and Specialisation"; lesson and meta: "1.1 Cell Structure"
build_log.deck_does: Uses Sub-Strand 1.1 Cell Structure from the lesson data. The deck does not show the 1.3 label.
build_log.why: The sub-strand number does not match between the unit data and the lesson data. SoW owner to check.

build_log.sow_says: "A Form 1 student in Nairobi cuts their finger" (anchoring phenomenon)
build_log.deck_does: Refers to Amina, as the lesson plan does. The deck never says Form 1.
build_log.why: CBE uses Grade 10, not Form 1. The SoW owner should update the phenomenon text.

build_log.sow_says: keyInquiry: "What are the structural differences between plant and animal cells?"
build_log.deck_does: Teaches prokaryote versus eukaryote, as the activities do.
build_log.why: The key inquiry names plant and animal cells, but this lesson compares a bacterium with a human cheek cell. SoW owner to check.

build_log.sow_says: Overview: "identifying four key structural differences"; Observe lists five features (nucleus; organelles; size; cell wall; genetic material location)
build_log.deck_does: Shows all five rows in the table.
build_log.why: The number of features differs between the overview and the activity. The deck follows the Observe activity.

build_log.sow_says: "the cheek cell is about 50 times bigger than E. coli" (sizes given: 1–5 micrometres and 10–100 micrometres; teacher says E. coli is about 2 micrometres)
build_log.deck_does: Keeps the SoW wording for the cold-call question and the size ranges.

lesson_oneliner: Are the bacteria in a cut built like our own cells? Let us find out.
purpose: Students compare a bacterium (E. coli) with a human cheek cell. They use only the diagrams as evidence.
They find the structural differences themselves: nucleus, organelles, size, cell wall and where the DNA is.
This matters because it links to the healing cut. The bacteria that could infect Amina's finger are built differently from her own body cells.
This lesson prepares students for Lessons 4 and 5, where they go inside plant and animal cells.
before_class: Prepare the two diagrams (E. coli and cheek cell) as printed copies if you can. If not, plan to flip between the two diagram slides.
Prepare the comparison table in notebooks, either pre-printed or drawn on the board for students to copy.
Check the class register. Mark five students for the cold-call round and three for the prediction share. Spread them across groups and seating zones.
Find the Lesson 1 wonder notes on the Driving Question Board. Pick two or three that today's work can answer.
Have sticky notes or small pieces of paper ready (one per student).
Draw two columns on the Driving Question Board: WHAT WE NOW KNOW and WHAT WE STILL WONDER.
Remind students to bring their Version 1 cell model from Lesson 2 and red, blue and black pencils or pens.
Check that the ARES links work offline before class. Do not open any of them until the times named below.
do_not_show: Do not show the slide 'E. coli: how is it built?' or the cheek cell slide until students have written and shared their predictions.
Do not show the slide 'Words that carry their meaning' until students have written their three sentences.
Do not open the ARES video or reading links for prokaryotes and eukaryotes until students have finished their own table. They give away the answers.
Keep the answer keys in the notes only. Do not write the table answers on the board before the class review.
so_far: You have met the healing cut and learned that a cell is the basic unit of life.
goals: Compare two types of cell using diagrams.
Complete a table of structural differences.
Explain why this matters for the healing cut.

summary.observe_prompt: Name the two cells you studied. What differences did you find?
summary.learn_prompt: How are prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells different? What do both have?
summary.explain_prompt: Are the bacteria in Amina's cut built like her own cells?
summary.next_lesson: We go inside a plant cell to find out what its parts do.
summary.answer_observe: I studied two labelled diagrams: E. coli, a bacterium linked to food poisoning from nyama choma, and a human cheek cell. E. coli has no membrane-bound nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. It has a cell wall and is about 1–5 micrometres. The cheek cell has a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. It has no cell wall and is about 10–100 micrometres.
summary.answer_learn: Prokaryotic cells, such as E. coli, have no membrane-bound nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Their DNA lies free in a nucleoid region. Eukaryotic cells, such as human cheek cells, have a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Prokaryotes are generally much smaller (1–5 micrometres) than eukaryotes (10–100 micrometres). Both cell types contain ribosomes, but ribosomes are not membrane-bound.
summary.answer_explain: The bacteria that could infect Amina's cut, such as E. coli, are prokaryotes. They are built much more simply than her own body cells, which are eukaryotes. In eukaryotes, the membrane-bound nucleus keeps the DNA in its own compartment, which supports the complex jobs needed for healing. This structural difference shows that bacteria and body cells are both alive but behave very differently. It also explains why Amina's white blood cells, which are eukaryotes, can find and destroy E. coli in the wound.
reflection: Did the cold-call questions show any confusion between ribosomes (in both cells, not membrane-bound) and membrane-bound organelles? If so, begin Lesson 4 with a 2-minute clarification using the ribosome row of the table.
Did students link E. coli to the healing cut in Sentence 3, or did they treat it as abstract? If the link was weak, make the bridge clear again at the start of Lesson 4.
Did the wonder notes show readiness to ask what organelles do, or do students still not know what a membrane-bound organelle is? Use this to set the depth of diagram work in Lesson 4.
Were the five cold-called students from different groups, seating zones and genders? Check the register and adjust the call pattern in Lesson 4.

notes.why_this_works: Writing about observing, learning and explaining in three steps moves students from what they saw to why it matters. Returning to Amina's cut keeps the anchor phenomenon alive.

say: Here is our journey through this unit. Today is Lesson 3.
So far we have met the healing cut, and we have said a cell is the basic unit of life.
Today we ask: are all cells built the same way? Keep our big question in your mind: why do cells look so different?
unit_map_notes.why_this_works: A quick look at the whole unit shows students where today fits. It links each lesson to the one anchor question, so the work feels like one story.

do: Read the three goals aloud.
Read the four key words with their meanings. Do not explain more.
Do not add any words about bacteria or nuclei. Students will find those in the evidence.
say: By the end of today you can compare two types of cell using diagrams. You can complete a table of differences. And you can explain why it matters for Amina's cut.
These four words will help you today: structure, evidence, compare and micrometre. A micrometre is one millionth of a metre. It is a very small unit.
goals_notes.why_this_works: Goals tell students what success looks like. Choosing words that do not give away the result keeps the discovery for the lesson itself.
